extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of theology, biblical interpretation, and 17th-century political/theological theory
extracted.subtask_description: Close exegetical guidance from a 17th‑century theological/political treatise on how to read biblical texts about eternal life, hell, church, salvation, and related doctrines. Emphasizes contextual, metaphorical, and scripturally grounded interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret 'die' as mortality/certainty of death
rubrics_metrics.description: "When it is said, 'In the day that thou eatest thereof, thou shalt surely die,' it must needs bee meant of his Mortality, and certitude of death."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not take the Genesis phrase as immediate physical cessation; read it as loss of immortality (mortality entering upon Adam and his posterity). Use contextual facts (e.g., Adam lived after eating and had children) to determine intended sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use internal comparisons (Adam/Christ) for inferencing the place of eternal life
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument from Romans/1 Corinthians: "As by the offence of one, Judgment came upon all men to condemnation, even so by the righteousnesse of one, the free gift came upon all men to Justification of Life"; "For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When Scripture makes explicit comparisons, maintain logical consistency across the comparison: if Adam's forfeited life was on Earth, then Christ's restored life should be understood analogously (i.e., earthly), unless other texts plainly contradict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read geographic and cultic place‑words literally where context points to real locations (Zion = Jerusalem = Earth)
rubrics_metrics.description: "'Upon Zion God commanded the blessing, even Life for evermore;' for Zion, is in Jerusalem, upon Earth"; New Jerusalem is described as "coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a Bride" (Rev.21) and therefore interpreted as descending to Earth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the plain referent of place‑words (Zion, Jerusalem, Mount Zion) unless scriptural context forces a different reading; prophetic imagery that describes the city 'coming down' supports an earthly seat of God's Kingdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat metaphors for Hell (fire, lake, darkness, Tartarus, Gehenna) as non‑literal and seek their proper sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages describing "Lake that burneth with Fire and Brimstone," "Utter Darknesse," "Inferno/Tartarus," and related imagery are often metaphorical and derive from historical/typical events (Sodom, Tophet, Egyptian darkness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume metaphors denote a specific physical place or physical mode of torment; interpret them as signifying destruction, shame, separation from God's elect, or other real effects. Identify the real ground behind metaphorical language (e.g., Sodom→destruction; Tophet→filth/fires; darkness→separation/outside habitation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate and interpret names like 'Satan', 'Devil', 'Abbadon' as offices/appellatives, not proper individual names
rubrics_metrics.description: "Satan, Devill, Abbadon, set not forth to us any Individuall person... but onely an office, or quality; and are therefore Appellatives; which ought not to have been left untranslated..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rendering these terms as titles (the Enemy, the Accuser, the Destroyer) prevents importing pagan daemonology and helps identify them as roles (earthly enemies of God's kingdom) rather than distinct supernatural persons without clear scriptural warrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand 'torments of Hell' imagery as expressing grief, shame, conscience, social/political calamity, and 'second death'
rubrics_metrics.description: Torments described by "weeping, and gnashing of teeth," "the worm of Conscience," "Fire," and "Shame, and contempt" are said to "design metaphorically a grief, and discontent of mind, from the sight of that Eternall felicity in others..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read such imagery as depicting moral/psychological and societal consequences (loss, shame, contempt, bondage under bad rulers) and as an estate that may culminate in a 'Second Death' (final destruction), rather than necessarily implying literal eternal conscious unending bodily suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish immortality of the soul from immortality of the whole person (resurrection)
rubrics_metrics.description: "That the Soul of man is in its own nature Eternall... is a doctrine not apparent in Scripture... The Immortall Life... beginneth not in man, till the Resurrection, and day of Judgment."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conflating passages about the soul with teaching about the resurrection of the person; where Scripture emphasizes 'resurrection of the body' treat personal immortality as tied to the resurrection rather than inherent to human nature independent of divine promise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require scriptural evidence before positing extra‑scriptural cosmological doctrines (e.g., Empyrean heaven)
rubrics_metrics.description: References to a 'Caelum Empyreum' have "no mention in Scripture, nor ground in Reason" and thus are not easily drawn from texts; 'Kingdome of Heaven' may mean God's rule over people rather than ascent to an aetherial region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept cosmological claims (higher heavens, places above the stars) without clear scriptural warrant; prefer readings grounded in Scripture and reason rather than later theological or pagan cosmologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define 'Salvation' broadly as remission of sin and deliverance from death/misery (eternal life)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The joyes of Life Eternall, are in Scripture comprehended all under the name of SALVATION... To be saved, is to be secured... comprehending Want, Sicknesse, and Death it self."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting salvific language, read forgiveness of sins, healing, deliverance from enemies, and final eternal life as facets of one salvific reality; cross‑reference healings and pardons in the Gospels as equivalent signs of salvation (e.g., forgiveness vs. healing of the palsied man).

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand 'Redemption' / 'Ransome' as that which God requires (not a market‑value equivalence) and OT sacrifices as accepted types/means
rubrics_metrics.description: "By this Ransome, is not intended a satisfaction for Sin, equivalent to the Offence... The dammage a man does to another, he may make amends for by restitution... but sin cannot be taken away by recompence... But sins may bee pardoned... Gratis, or upon such penalty, as God is pleased to accept."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret ransom/sacrifice language as describing what divine justice and mercy require; do not attempt to compute equivalence between offense and price. Treat Old Testament sacrifices as the forms God accepted prior to Christ, typological rather than economically compensatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret the multiple senses of 'church' by context (temple/edifice, congregation assembled, whole Christian multitude, elect, particular local church)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The word Church... Sometimes... it is taken for Gods House... It is taken also sometimes for the men that have right to be of the Congregation... Sometimes also for the Elect onely... Sometimes, for a Congregation assembled..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine which sense is intended case‑by‑case from grammatical and situational context (e.g., 'the Church that is in his house' vs. 'A Glorious Church... meant of the Church Triumphant'). Do not assume a single uniform meaning across all texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read prophetic and eschatological 'world' language in its tripartite scriptural scheme (Old World, Present World, World to Come)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three worlds in Scripture: the Old World (Adam→Flood), the Present World (Jesus: 'My Kingdome is not of this World'), and the World to Come ('we... look for new Heavens, and a new Earth').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this tripartite framework when interpreting 'world to come' passages: expect the promise of new heavens and a new earth (eschatological renewal) rather than unmoored speculations about other realms; link 'world to come' to resurrection, final judgment, and God's renewed kingdom.
